paragraphs.title: Justice Required in the Royal House and the Threat of Destruction

answers: The house of the king of Judah
easy.explanation: The Lord told Jeremiah to go down to the house of the king of Judah.
easy.q: Where was Jeremiah told to go?

easy.explanation: They were commanded to execute judgment and righteousness.
easy.q: What were the king, his servants, and the people commanded to do?

answers: The stranger, the fatherless, and the widow
easy.explanation: The Lord forbade violence against the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow.
easy.q: Whom were they forbidden to oppress or harm?

answers: Kings of David's line would continue to sit on the throne
The people would move to another land
medium.explanation: Kings would enter through the gates and sit on the throne of David.
medium.q: What would happen if they obeyed the command?

answers: Rescue what was taken from the oppressed
Defend the city from an enemy
medium.explanation: The command was to rescue the spoiled from the oppressor.
medium.q: What does “deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor” mean?

answers: The house would become a desolation
medium.explanation: The Lord swore that the house would become a desolation.
medium.q: What would happen if they refused to hear the Lord's words?

answers: Because its people forsook the Lord's covenant and served other gods
challenge.explanation: The nations would identify abandonment of the covenant and idolatry as the cause.
challenge.q: Why would many nations ask why the city was destroyed?

answers: Justice is presented as a condition for the continuation of David's royal house
challenge.explanation: Obedience would allow kings of David's line to continue sitting on the throne.
challenge.q: What connection is shown between justice and the continuation of David's rule?

answers: The destruction of the royal house's splendor
challenge.explanation: The choice cedars cast into the fire symbolize the destruction of the royal house.
challenge.q: What do the cut-down cedars cast into the fire represent?

paragraphs.title: Shallum and the Exile from Which There Is No Return

answers: The one going away into exile
easy.explanation: They were told to weep for the one going away rather than for the dead.
easy.q: For whom were the people told not to weep as for the dead?

answers: Josiah's son and king of Judah
easy.explanation: Shallum is identified as the son of Josiah, king of Judah.
He would see his native country no more.
easy.q: What would Shallum never see again?

answers: For the one who was going away
medium.explanation: The passage says to weep sore for him that goeth away.
medium.q: For whom were the people told to weep sore?

answers: One who is taken into exile
One who travels among Judah's cities
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to Shallum being taken away from the land.
medium.q: What does “him that goeth away” mean in this passage?

medium.explanation: The prophecy says, “He shall die in the place whither they have led him captive.”
medium.q: What would happen to Shallum in the place where he was taken captive?

answers: The dead person has already died, while Shallum goes into exile and will not return
The dead person returns, while Shallum remains in Judah
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts ordinary mourning with grief for an exile who will never return.
challenge.q: What is the main difference between the dead person and Shallum?

answers: That his exile is temporary and easy
That his exile is a complete separation from his homeland
That he will rule Judah from far away
challenge.explanation: Not seeing the land again emphasizes the severity of his exile.
challenge.q: What does Shallum's never seeing his native country emphasize?

answers: The grief is directed toward someone still living but being taken into exile
challenge.explanation: The command distinguishes mourning for the dead from sorrow over the living exile.
challenge.q: Why is “Weep ye not for the dead” unusual in this context?

easy.explanation: He said, “I will build me a wide house and large chambers.”

answers: He used their service without wages
easy.explanation: He used his neighbour's service without wages and did not give him his work's payment.
easy.q: How did he treat his workers?

easy.explanation: His father is described as doing judgment and justice.

answers: Jehoiakim pursued luxury and oppression, while his father practiced justice
Jehoiakim was poor, while his father was rich
Jehoiakim left the throne, while his father stayed in exile
medium.explanation: Jehoiakim's unjust building is contrasted with his father's just rule.
medium.q: What contrast is made between Jehoiakim and his father?

medium.explanation: The phrase means that the house was built through injustice and oppression.
medium.q: What does “by unrighteousness” mean in “buildeth his house by unrighteousness”?

answers: To criticize his trust in outward luxury instead of justice
To command him to cut cedars
medium.explanation: The question exposes the emptiness of relying on luxurious surroundings.
medium.q: Why was Jehoiakim asked, “Shalt thou reign, because thou closest thyself in cedar?”

answers: Judging the cause of the poor and needy
challenge.explanation: Judging the cause of the poor and needy is presented as knowing the Lord.
challenge.q: What did the Lord say was “to know me”?

answers: Only the size of his house
Covetousness, shedding innocent blood, oppression, and violence
challenge.explanation: The Lord lists his covetousness, bloodshed, oppression, and violence.

answers: It was splendid but built through injustice
It was simple but full of righteousness
It was built by foreign enemies
challenge.explanation: The outward splendor concealed the oppression used to create it.
challenge.q: What contrast is shown between the palace's appearance and its moral value?

paragraphs.title: Jerusalem's Cry and the Breaking of Her Allies

answers: In Lebanon, Bashan, and from the passages
easy.explanation: Jerusalem was told to go up to Lebanon, cry in Bashan, and lift up her voice from the passages.
easy.q: Where was Jerusalem told to cry?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “all thy lovers are destroyed.”

answers: She asked for a new king
easy.q: How did Jerusalem respond when the Lord spoke in her prosperity?

answers: She would be ashamed and confounded for her wickedness
medium.explanation: The prophecy says she would be ashamed and confounded for all her wickedness.
medium.q: What would result from Jerusalem's refusal to hear?

medium.explanation: The term refers to those who supported or allied themselves with Jerusalem.
medium.q: What do “thy lovers” mean in this context?

answers: The wind would carry them away, and her lovers would go into captivity
medium.explanation: The wind would eat up her pastors, and her lovers would go into captivity.
medium.q: What would happen to Jerusalem's pastors?

answers: She trusted in impressive surroundings that could not save her
She had become a desert city
challenge.explanation: The cedar nest represents false security in wealth and luxury.
challenge.q: What does Jerusalem's nest among the cedars suggest about her security?

answers: Jerusalem refused to hear during prosperity, and distress followed
challenge.explanation: Her refusal to listen during prosperity is followed by shame and coming distress.
challenge.q: How are prosperity and distress connected in the prophecy?

answers: The building of a new palace
challenge.explanation: The image communicates intense pain and trouble.
challenge.q: What does the image of pain like a woman in travail express?

The Lord said He would give him into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans.
easy.q: Into whose hand would Coniah be given?

easy.explanation: The prophecy says, “I will cast thee out, and thy mother that bare thee.”
easy.q: Who would be cast out with Coniah?

He would become stronger on his throne
He would reign in another land

challenge.q: What contrast is found between the signet and the broken vessel?

answers: The irrevocable nature of their exile
Their rule in a foreign land
challenge.explanation: The prophecy plainly says they will not return to the land they desire.
challenge.q: What does their not returning to the desired land emphasize?

answers: To emphasize his humiliation and loss of royal honor
To describe the building of his palace

challenge.q: Why is Coniah compared to a despised broken vessel?

paragraphs.title: The Land's Verdict and the End of the Dynasty

easy.explanation: The prophecy addresses the earth three times and commands it to hear.
easy.q: Who was told to hear the word of the Lord?

answers: As childless, a man who would not prosper in his days
As a king who would return
easy.explanation: The Lord says to write him as childless and as a man who would not prosper.

answers: None would rule on David's throne
They would immediately return to the land
easy.explanation: No man of his seed would prosper while sitting on David's throne or ruling Judah.
easy.q: What would happen to Coniah's descendants?

answers: Even if he had children, none of his descendants would rule on David's throne
He could not have any children according to the verse
medium.explanation: The following words explain that the issue is the failure of his descendants to rule.
medium.q: What does “childless” mean in relation to the dynasty?

answers: He would not succeed during his lifetime
He would be unable to speak
medium.explanation: The phrase describes failure during the period of his life.
medium.q: What does “shall not prosper in his days” mean?

answers: No descendant of Coniah would sit upon it
Coniah would sit upon it forever
The throne would be transferred to Babylon
medium.explanation: The prophecy denies his descendants a successful reign on David's throne.
medium.q: What judgment is pronounced concerning David's throne?

answers: It emphasizes that the whole land is called to witness the judgment
challenge.explanation: The repetition gives solemn emphasis to the declaration concerning Coniah.
challenge.q: Why does the repeated address “O earth, earth, earth” strengthen the prophecy?

answers: The end of his descendants' rule in Judah
The immediate restoration of his kingdom
challenge.explanation: The prophecy removes the possibility of his descendants ruling Judah.
challenge.q: What was the result of the judgment concerning Coniah for Judah's government?

answers: Exile brings not only removal from the land but also the loss of continuing royal rule
Exile has no connection with the throne
